newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Bit by bit, Hungary sells off "dinosaurs".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bit by bit, Hungary sells off "dinosaurs".

text.p: Dunaferr steel mill, built under communist rule in a spot with no iron ore, is as unlikely a prospect for a privatisation success story as any in Hungary.

Hungary's fourth biggest manufacturing company, employing some 11,000 people on the banks of the Danube 80 km (50 miles) south of Budapest, Dunaferr essentially went bankrupt in 1993 when the embargo of Yugoslavia cut its main transport route.
"All our basic raw materials were transported on the Danube and all our exports to the Far East were shipped by river," said Istvan Horvath, Dunaferr's chief executive officer.
"By the middle of 1993 the company became insolvent."
DUNAFERR FORCED TO SCRAP RENOVATION

A fancy bit of book-keeping rescued Dunaferr by allowing it to capitalise billions of forints it owed the government, an official source said. But the mill was forced to scrap a planned renovation and has had to cope with outdated Soviet equipment.

"Dunaferr is a hopeless company in my opinion," said Peter Mihalyi, a former official of Hungary's state privatisation agency APV Rt and now a professor in the department of economics of the Central European University.
And yet Mihalyi is not alone in thinking that Dunaferr, along with other industrial "dinosaurs" that fell on hard times when communism collapsed, could find a buyer.

A management team that won a contract to run Dunaferr for five years is breaking it into smaller companies, spinning off non-core businesses and starting promising new ones, including the biggest flat-panel radiator plant in eastern Europe.

The changes have allowed Dunaferr, one of Hungary's biggest exporters, to boost turnover threefold since 1991 and project a pre-tax profit of 7.144 billion forints in 1997, although management admits it is running old equipment into the ground.
DEBATE OVER PRIVATISATION TIMING
Horvath, a veteran Dunaferr manager who heads the team that took over the management of the company last year, thinks the time is not yet right to privatise Dunaferr.
"I have tried to find a strategic investor, but when I tried no strategic investor anywhere in the world was interested in Dunaferr," he told Reuters.

"Obviously if there is no strategic investor, then there's no bank loan either. And it would be dangerous to take Dunaferr on the stock exchange at the moment, because its financial position is not strong enough."
Mihalyi disagrees.
"Let's have a fair tender (offer) and see what the market says," he told Reuters in an interview.
"The Hungarian economy is now in good shape, we get a good international press...I can imagine that, given the good climate now, there would be some interesting offers. So let's try."
A privatisation of Dunaferr is not in the APV Rt's official prospectus of 1997 offerings, and APV officials have said they will let the management contract run its full five years.
But the unexpected has been happening in this year that is supposed to be the last big one for Hungarian privatisations.
In late June the government ordered APV to try again to sell busmaker Ikarus Rt IKAR.CN with a tender offer in August.
IKARUS BUSMAKER STRUGGLES TO BREAK EVEN
One of the world's biggest busmakers in communist times, Ikarus is saddled with mammoth production lines no one wants and sparked virtually no interest in a tender offer last year.
In an interview, APV officials said sales last year of only 800 buses had left Ikarus on the verge of collapse, but increased sales this year should allow it to break even.
In addition, a government injection of eight billion forints for restructuring, including a reduction of about 600 administrative staff, has made the company more competitive.

"Last year's production (of 800 buses) was a serious situation for the company, we saw that the company would collapse," Balint Kerdo, an APV official in charge of the Ikarus privatisation, told Reuters.

"This year we can see that the company will reach a breakeven point...with between 1,500 and 2,000 buses. This quantity is good enough to break even, just before a profit," added APV deputy managing director Peter Endrody.
"That's why we thought that it is better to release the company from state ownership to make it easier for the management to realise this programmme."

Ikarus, like Dunaferr, has also been farmed out by APV to an assets management team. At Ikarus, the team is headed by entrepreneur Gabor Szeles, who engineered the rescue of the bankrupt state electronics firm Videoton.
Although the management teams have improved the balance sheets, critics say the arrangement delays the inevitable day of reckoning.
PRIVATISATION PARTNERS SOUGHT

Mihalyi said the companies under asset management, along with other state-owned companies that have not been tendered, are in a state of "privatisation limbo": Banks won't lend to them, good people leave and legal entanglements pile up.
"I can tell you 50 cases where (state-owned) companies were in quite okay situations a year ago but they are in much worse shape today," he said.
Tamas Kirilly, an official at the Industry and Trade Ministry who oversees some of the big industrial concerns, said the management deals may have given beleaguered companies a new lease on life.
He is sceptical of some of Szeles's sales claims, but said the management team at Dunaferr knows that the plant can only be saved if a buyer is eventually found.

"It's not in their interest to block anything because money is needed to upgrade the technology," he said. "The management knows that if they don't find an owner with a lot of money, the Hungarian government has no money to transform the steel works.
"So it's in their basic interest to find a privatisation partner."
